name: Hà Giang
known_for: The Đồng Văn karst plateau and the loop road around it. Mã Pì Lèng, the pass above the Nho Quế gorge, is the highest and narrowest piece of road in the country. Markets in Mèo Vạc and Đồng Văn still trade livestock and indigo, not souvenirs.
best_months: September to November, and March to April
best_note: Buckwheat flowers on the plateau through late October and November; the gorge is clearest in the dry months.
avoid: June to August. The summer rain brings landslides onto the Mã Pì Lèng road and the pass closes for days at a time.
getting_there: Nội Bài (Hà Nội) is the airport, then 300 km north by road — 6 to 7 hours by sleeper bus or car to Hà Giang city, and the loop starts there.
opinion: Four days is the shortest honest loop. Three means riding in the dark.

name: Sa Pa
known_for: Rice terraces stacked down the Mường Hoa valley, and Fansipan above them at 3,143 m. The town itself has been built over twice in twenty years; the valley has not.
best_months: March to May, and September to November
best_note: The terraces are flooded and mirrored in April and May, and gold from mid-September for about three weeks.
avoid: July and August — the heaviest rain of the year lands on the domestic holiday peak, and the valley paths turn to clay.
getting_there: Nội Bài (Hà Nội), then the Lào Cai expressway: 320 km, about 5 hours by road. The night train to Lào Cai leaves 38 km of mountain road to finish.
opinion: Sleep in the valley, not in the town. We think that is the whole difference.

name: Mộc Châu
known_for: A dairy and tea plateau in Sơn La, in the northwest — they call it the white meadowland. Tea hills laid out in rings, plum orchards in the valleys, and almost no foreign visitors on an ordinary weekday.
best_note: Plum blossom through late January and February; the white mustard flowers come in November.
avoid: June to August. The rain is constant and the plateau sits in haze, which is the one thing it has nothing to offer in.
getting_there: Nội Bài (Hà Nội), then west on Highway 6 through Hòa Bình — about 220 km from the airport, 4 to 5 hours by car or bus.
opinion: The best stop between Hà Nội and the northwest, and poor as a destination in itself.

name: Hạ Long
known_for: A bay of some 1,900 limestone islets over 1,553 km², on the UNESCO list since 1994. The famous water is the 334 km² core; the quieter water is east of it, towards Bái Tử Long.
best_months: October to December, and March to April
best_note: Clear air and a flat sea; the haze that sits on the bay in spring lifts by late March.
avoid: July to September — typhoon season. Sailings are cancelled at a few hours' notice and the port does not refund the weather.
getting_there: Cát Bi (Hải Phòng) is the nearest airport at 75 km; most people fly to Nội Bài and drive the expressway, 170 km in about 2 hours 30.
opinion: One night on the water is enough. Two is the same view with a second dinner.

name: Cát Bà
known_for: The largest of 367 islands at the southeastern edge of Lan Hạ bay, a UNESCO biosphere reserve since 2004 and part of the world heritage site since 2023. Half of it is national park; Cao Vọng, at 322 m, looks over the lot.
best_months: April to June, and September to October
best_note: Warm water without the crowd, and the forest paths are dry enough to walk.
avoid: July and August. The domestic holiday fortnight fills every room in Cát Bà town and the harbour front is shoulder to shoulder.
getting_there: Cát Bi (Hải Phòng), 45 km to the ferry at Got and a 20-minute crossing. From Hà Nội it is about 3 hours door to door.
opinion: Better value than Hạ Long for the same water, and you sleep on land.

name: Ninh Bình
known_for: Limestone towers standing in rice fields, with rivers running through caves at their feet. Tràng An, Tam Cốc–Bích Động and the old capital at Hoa Lư were listed together by UNESCO in 2014, 6,226 hectares of it. The rowers use their legs, not their arms.
best_months: February to April, and late May
best_note: The rice at Tam Cốc turns gold for about ten days around the end of May. The rest of the spring is green and cool.
avoid: June to August — flat heat over open water with no shade on the boats.
getting_there: Nội Bài (Hà Nội), then south on the expressway — about 130 km from the airport, 2 hours by road. The Tràng An wharf is 7 km west of Ninh Bình town; the north–south train stops in the town.
opinion: Possible in a day from Hà Nội, and much better with a night in it.

name: Phong Nha
known_for: Phong Nha–Kẻ Bàng, 857 km² of karst with around 300 known caves, on the UNESCO list since 2003. Sơn Đoòng, found by a local man and surveyed in 2009, is the largest cave passage in the world.
best_note: The river caves are open and the water inside them is low enough to walk.
avoid: October and November. The floods come through the valley, the river caves shut, and the expedition operators stop running.
getting_there: Đồng Hới (VDH) is 45 km away, about an hour by road. The north–south train also stops at Đồng Hới.
opinion: The one place on this list where we would spend money on a guide rather than a hotel.

name: Huế
known_for: The Nguyễn capital: a walled citadel on the north bank of the Perfume River, and the emperors' tombs spread through the hills south of it. The food is its own cuisine, not a regional version of anyone else's.
best_note: The only reliably dry stretch of the year here, and the tombs are walkable before the heat.
avoid: September to December. Huế is the wettest city in Vietnam and in October and November the river comes over the bank.
getting_there: Phú Bài (HUI) sits in the southeast of the city, about 15 km from the citadel — 25 minutes by road. From Đà Nẵng the train over the Hải Vân pass takes about 2 hours 30 and is worth taking for its own sake.
opinion: Two days, and give one of them to the tombs rather than the citadel.

name: Hội An
known_for: A trading port that was left alone for two hundred years, so its merchant houses, assembly halls and Japanese bridge are still standing. UNESCO listed the old town in 1999. An Bàng beach is four kilometres away.
best_note: Dry, warm, and the sea is calm enough to swim before the summer heat arrives.
avoid: October and November. The Thu Bồn rises and the old town floods — shops board up and boats work the streets.
getting_there: Đà Nẵng (DAD) is 30 km north, about 45 minutes by road. There is no station in Hội An; the train stops in Đà Nẵng.
opinion: Walk the old town before seven in the morning. After nine it belongs to the tour groups.

name: Quy Nhơn
known_for: A working port city with a long curved beach in front of it, Chăm towers behind it, and the Eo Gió headland and Kỳ Co cove to the north. It has not been built up the way Nha Trang and Đà Nẵng were.
best_note: A dry, steady season with a flat sea — the south central coast runs later than the north.
avoid: October to December — the wet months here, with a rough sea and the boats to Kỳ Co often not running.
getting_there: Phù Cát (UIH) is 30 km north of the city, about 45 minutes. The train stops at Diêu Trì, 10 km out.
opinion: The best seafood on this list, and we are not going to pretend that is a fact.

name: Đà Lạt
known_for: A hill town at 1,500 m in the Lâm Viên plateau, built by the French as an escape from the Saigon heat. Pines, a lake, flower farms and coffee grown on the slopes around it.
best_note: The dry season: cold mornings, clear afternoons, and the hills around the town are walkable.
avoid: June to September. The afternoon rain is reliable and heavy, and it takes the view with it.
getting_there: Liên Khương (DLI) is 30 km south, about 40 minutes up the pass. From Hồ Chí Minh City it is 300 km, 7 hours by bus.
opinion: Skip the attractions in the town. The farms and the pass roads are why you came.

name: Mũi Né
known_for: Red and white sand dunes behind a fishing village, and the most dependable cross-shore wind in the country — which is why the kitesurfing season here is a season and not a weekend.
best_note: The dry months, and the wind that makes the place runs through them.
avoid: June to September — the wet season, with the wind gone and the sea brown after rain.
getting_there: Tân Sơn Nhất (Hồ Chí Minh City) is the airport; the Phan Thiết expressway brings it to about 3 hours 30 for 200 km.
opinion: Two days unless you kite, in which case stay a fortnight.

name: Phú Quốc
known_for: The largest island in Vietnam at 575 km², in the Gulf of Thailand. The north is national park and pepper farms; the south has the beaches, the fish sauce houses and most of the building work.
best_note: The dry monsoon: flat sea, clear water, and the boats to the An Thới islands run every day.
avoid: July to September. The southwest monsoon puts a swell on the west coast and the sand goes grey with it.
getting_there: Phú Quốc (PQC) is on the island, 10 km from Dương Đông — an hour from Hồ Chí Minh City by air. Ferries run from Rạch Giá and Hà Tiên.
opinion: Stay north of the airport. The south end is a building site with a beach attached.

name: Côn Đảo
known_for: Sixteen islands 185 km off Vũng Tàu, with 8,800 people on them. A national park above and below the water, the prison the French and then the Americans ran, and green turtles nesting on Bảy Cạnh.
best_note: The calmest sea of the year. Turtles come ashore on Bảy Cạnh from June to September.
avoid: September to November. The crossing turns rough, ferries are cancelled at short notice and the small aircraft go with them.
getting_there: Côn Đảo (VCS) takes an hour from Hồ Chí Minh City on a turboprop. The ferry from Sóc Trăng takes about 2 hours 45.
opinion: Give an afternoon to the prison and the cemetery. It is the reason the island is quiet.
